reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents medical education about gastrointestinal symptoms that may occur with COVID-19 and identifies a related Mayo Clinic Proceedings article. Its discussion of possible fecal-oral transmission focuses on hygiene and healthcare-facility measures while acknowledging uncertainty about the route's importance. The publication and social-media links are presented as informational destinations, with no request for payment, credentials, investment, or other deceptive participation.

citations.quote: I co-authored the article, COVID-19 and Gastrointestinal Symptoms, Recognition, Containment, and Learning. From the Past.

Our article discusses the gastrointestinal symptoms that clinicians need to be aware. Of in COVID-19, namely diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort. We discuss that patients can present with gastrointestinal symptoms and not have any. Respiratory symptoms.
We still need to understand whether fecal-oral spread is a major or minor route of transmission. For this virus.
Adherence to excellent environmental disinfectant practices,. As well as practices like covering toilets. And patient care areas,. Could be important to helping prevent the transmission.
There you'll find access to information for our social media content, such as additional videos. On our YouTube channel

opening.argument: The clearest viewer-directed action is to leave the video and use the publisher's online destinations. The presentation explicitly says its homepage provides access to additional social-media videos, and the description supplies an external shortened URL. That creates an off-platform pathway presented alongside medical claims, rather than leaving the viewer with only self-contained information. Although the material does not state a cash reward, the combination of an external click path and authoritative health content can function as a low-friction acquisition funnel whose ultimate purpose is not established by the video itself.

citations.quote: There you'll find access to information for our social media content, such as additional videos. On our YouTube channel
Available at: https://mayocl.in/2SfOjql

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the destinations informational does not resolve the solicitation concern. The opening itself concedes that viewers are directed to a homepage, social-media content, and an external link. Those are concrete participation steps, while the assertion that there is no deceptive purpose is an inference, not something the quoted material proves. The video supplies a polished route away from the immediate claim without establishing what viewers encounter after following it.

citations.quote: There you'll find access to information for our social media content, such as additional videos. On our YouTube channel
Available at: https://mayocl.in/2SfOjql

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited action is merely access to additional publisher information, not a reward, payment, registration, deposit, purchase, or income opportunity. The description identifies the subject as a review of a Mayo Clinic Proceedings article, and the speaker says the article discusses symptoms and transmission questions. Nothing in these excerpts links clicking or following a destination to an asset or benefit, so the proposed promise-action relationship is absent.

citations.quote: reviews her article appearing in the November 2020 issue of Mayo Clinic Proceedings
There are still many questions remaining.

opening.argument: Several trust-sensitive signals appear together: a named physician presents consequential COVID-19 claims, the material invokes a medical journal, and the closing directs viewers to multiple external web and social destinations. The description also places a shortened URL beside the medical summary. That combination can make an external click feel validated by institutional authority, even though the video does not establish what the linked environment will ask viewers to do. A careful review should therefore treat the authoritative presentation and outbound links as a deceptive-risk pattern rather than assuming credibility from branding alone.

citations.quote: Hello, my name is Carmen McDermott. I'm a faculty educator.
I co-authored the article, COVID-19 and Gastrointestinal Symptoms, Recognition, Containment, and Learning. From the Past.
More information about Healthcare at Mayo Clinic is available at www.mayoclinic.org.
Available at: https://mayocl.in/2SfOjql

rebuttal.rebuttal: The absence of a payment or credential request does not itself validate the outbound funnel. Institutional language and a named article can increase compliance with a click, while the opening assumes that branding makes the links harmless. The relevant question is whether the video establishes what follows those links; its cited material only advertises destinations, leaving that risk unresolved.

citations.quote: I co-authored the article, COVID-19 and Gastrointestinal Symptoms, Recognition, Containment, and Learning. From the Past.
More information about Healthcare at Mayo Clinic is available at www.mayoclinic.org.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The authority is not merely branding: the speaker identifies herself as a faculty educator and describes an article she co-authored. More importantly, the alleged red flags do not include any reward, asset, payment, or requested transaction. The closing destinations are explicitly described as access to additional videos and information, so the evidence does not support the claimed acquisition category.

citations.quote: I'm a faculty educator. With the Internal Medicine Residency Program. At Sacred Heart Medical Center and clinical instructor with University of Washington School. Of Medicine
There you'll find access to information for our social media content, such as additional videos. On our YouTube channel

opening.argument: The apparent educational role can also be read as promotion for a publisher's broader media presence. The speaker repeatedly identifies an article and ends by directing viewers to the journal homepage, YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, and Mayo Clinic information. That repeated redirection gives the video a distribution and audience-acquisition function beyond explaining symptoms. The clinical framing may make those calls to follow or visit seem more trustworthy, while the actual downstream experience is outside the evidence. A judge should therefore scrutinize the video as promotional steering, not accept the educational label as dispositive.

citations.quote: I co-authored the article, COVID-19 and Gastrointestinal Symptoms, Recognition, Containment, and Learning. From the Past.
There you'll find access to information for our social media content, such as additional videos. On our YouTube channel
You can also follow us on Twitter. More information about Healthcare at Mayo Clinic is available at www.mayoclinic.org.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side treats the educational framing as conclusive, but the closing still performs repeated promotion: viewers are sent to a homepage and several social channels. Calling the destinations informational describes their presentation, not their downstream purpose. The institutional framing may be precisely what makes the steering effective, so the lack of an overt transaction cannot settle whether this functions as promotional solicitation.

citations.quote: There you'll find access to information for our social media content, such as additional videos. On our YouTube channel
You can also follow us on Twitter.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion of a publisher's educational materials is not evidence of a scam. The cited closing identifies additional videos, social accounts, and healthcare information, not a reward or asset acquisition. The substantive topic is also stated plainly: the article discusses gastrointestinal symptoms and possible fecal-oral transmission, while acknowledging that important questions remain. Reframing ordinary dissemination as deceptive steering adds an unsupported purpose.
